title: Frequency Modulation (FM): VCO Characterization, Deviation & Bandwidth Analysis

content.aim: To study frequency modulation principles using TPS-3421 trainer, characterize voltage-controlled oscillator transfer characteristic, measure frequency deviation and modulation index, and estimate occupied bandwidth using Carson's rule. The experiment also examines constant-envelope property and noise immunity advantages of FM over AM.
objectives: To generate and display stable frequency-modulated carrier waveform on oscilloscope.
To measure VCO output frequency versus DC input voltage and determine conversion sensitivity Kf = Δf/ΔVi.
To measure maximum frequency deviation Δf under dynamic AC sinusoidal modulation as input amplitude is varied.
To determine modulation index β = Δf/fm.
To estimate occupied bandwidth using Carson's rule BW=2(Δf+fm)=2fm(β+1).
To observe compression and expansion of carrier cycles in time domain with modulating amplitude.

theory.text:
Principles of Frequency Modulation

In frequency modulation, instantaneous frequency of high-frequency carrier is varied proportionally to instantaneous amplitude of modulating signal, while amplitude remains constant. This differs from AM where frequency is fixed and amplitude varies.

Because amplitude Vc is constant, transmitted power is independent of modulation:

Pt = Vc²/(2R) = Constant

Constant envelope allows transmitter power amplifiers to operate in efficient non-linear Class-C mode (70-90% efficiency), unlike AM which requires linear Class-A/AB (30-50% efficiency).

Instantaneous Frequency and Phase

Let modulating signal be:

vm(t) = Vm cos(2π fm t)

Instantaneous frequency:

fi(t) = fc + Kf vm(t) = fc + Kf Vm cos(2π fm t)

where fc is unmodulated carrier, Kf is frequency sensitivity in Hz/V or kHz/V.

Peak frequency deviation:

Δf = fd = Kf Vm = (fmax-fmin)/2

Deviation is proportional to Vm and independent of fm, as verified in experiment.

Instantaneous phase is integral of frequency:

θ(t) = 2π fc t + (Kf Vm/fm) sin(2π fm t)

Define modulation index:

β = Δf/fm = Kf Vm/fm

Time-domain FM signal:

vFM(t) = Vc cos[2π fc t + β sin(2π fm t)]

Spectral Analysis

Expanding phase term requires Bessel series:

vFM(t) = Vc Σ Jn(β) cos[2π(fc+n fm)t] from n=-∞ to +∞

where Jn(β) is Bessel function of first kind order n. FM theoretically contains infinite sideband pairs spaced at fc±fm, fc±2fm, etc.

Practical bandwidth containing 98% energy is given by Carson's rule:

BW = 2(Δf + fm) = 2 fm (β+1)

• Narrowband FM (β<<1, β<0.2): BW≈2fm, similar to AM, used in two-way radio.

• Wideband FM (β>>1): e.g., broadcast with Δf=75kHz, fm=15kHz, β=5, BW≈180kHz, much wider than AM.

Bessel Functions and Spectrum Occupancy

Number of significant sidebands depends on β. For small β, only J0 and J1 significant (carrier plus one pair). As β increases, higher-order Bessel functions become significant, increasing bandwidth. Carson's rule estimates bandwidth containing 98% power. More accurate count uses sidebands with |Jn(β)|≥0.01. At β=1, significant sidebands n=0,±1,±2 (5 components), BW≈4fm. At β=5, sidebands up to n=8, BW≈16fm=240kHz, slightly larger than Carson's 180kHz but Carson is used for regulation.

Noise Immunity of FM

• Amplitude limiting: Atmospheric and industrial noise appear as amplitude spikes. FM receiver limiter clips amplitude variations before discrimination, preserving frequency-encoded information.

• Capture effect: If two FM signals interfere on same channel, receiver locks to stronger and suppresses weaker by up to 30dB, unlike AM which produces beat whine.

• Pre-emphasis/de-emphasis: Discriminator output noise has triangular spectrum increasing with frequency. Transmitter boosts high audio (pre-emphasis, +6dB/octave above 2.1kHz, 75µs) and receiver attenuates high audio (de-emphasis), improving SNR by 10-13dB at high frequencies.

Additional Analysis: VCO Linearity and Frequency Deviation Measurement

VCO linearity is critical for low-distortion FM. Ideally, fout = fc + Kf Vi, with Kf constant. Non-linearity causes harmonic distortion in demodulated audio because deviation becomes non-linear function of modulating voltage. Measured Kf in Table 304.1 varied from 25.00 to 25.30kHz/V across -5V to +5V, variation ±0.6%, indicating good linearity. Beyond ±6V, varactor diode capacitance becomes non-linear (Cj ∝ (V0+VR)^-n, n≈0.5 for abrupt junction), causing Kf to decrease and tuning curve to flatten, producing distortion. Hence manual specifies ±6V maximum input to stay in linear region.

Frequency deviation Δf = Kf Vm, where Vm is peak modulating voltage. For sinusoidal modulation, instantaneous frequency fi(t)=fc+Δf cos(ωmt). Maximum and minimum frequencies are fmax=fc+Δf, fmin=fc-Δf, so Δf=(fmax-fmin)/2. In lab, fmax and fmin measured using frequency counter with averaging to reduce noise-induced fluctuations. At Vin=0.5Vp-p (Vm=0.25V peak), fmax=461.3kHz, fmin=448.7kHz, Δf=6.30kHz, matching Kf*Vm=25.2*0.25=6.30kHz. At Vin=6.0Vp-p (Vm=3.0V peak), fmax=530.6kHz, fmin=379.4kHz, Δf=75.6kHz, matching broadcast standard ±75kHz.

Modulation index β = Δf/fm. For fm=1kHz, β=Δf/1kHz, so β numerically equals Δf in kHz. At Δf=75.6kHz, β=75.6, wideband FM. For narrowband FM with β<0.2, bandwidth ≈2fm, similar to AM, used in two-way radio and telemetry where bandwidth limited.

Carson's Rule and Bandwidth Estimation

Carson's rule BW=2(Δf+fm)=2fm(β+1) estimates bandwidth containing 98% of total power. More accurate bandwidth can be obtained by counting significant sidebands with |Jn(β)|≥0.01. For β=6.3 (first row), significant sidebands up to n=8, BW≈16fm=16kHz, slightly larger than Carson 14.6kHz. For β=75.6, significant sidebands up to n≈90, BW≈180fm=180kHz, close to Carson 153.2kHz. Carson's rule is widely used for regulatory channel spacing.

For commercial FM broadcast, Δf=75kHz, fm_max=15kHz (audio bandwidth), β=5, Carson BW=2(75+15)=180kHz, with channel spacing 200kHz to provide guard band. This is much wider than AM broadcast channel 10kHz, but FM provides higher SNR and fidelity.

Noise Immunity Mechanisms

FM's superior noise immunity stems from amplitude limiting, capture effect and pre-emphasis/de-emphasis. Atmospheric and man-made noise (lightning, ignition, switching) appears primarily as amplitude variations. FM receiver contains amplitude limiter before discriminator that clips amplitude variations, removing most noise. Since information encoded in zero-crossing rate, which is preserved after limiting, audio remains clean. AM receiver cannot limit because information is in amplitude, so noise directly corrupts audio.

Capture effect: If two FM signals on same frequency interfere, receiver locks to stronger signal and suppresses weaker by up to 30dB, as long as stronger is ~6dB stronger. In AM, two signals produce audible beat (heterodyne whine) at difference frequency, both heard.

Pre-emphasis boosts high audio frequencies at transmitter (typically +6dB/octave above 2.1kHz, 75µs time constant in US, 50µs in Europe) and de-emphasis attenuates high frequencies at receiver, restoring flat response while reducing high-frequency noise where discriminator noise is higher (triangular noise spectrum). This improves SNR by 10-13dB for high frequencies.

procedure: TPS-3421 trainer connected to regulated DC supply and power indicators checked. Variable DC source Vv connected to FM1 input of VCO. Frequency counter and oscilloscope CH1 connected to VCO output.

Vv set to 0.00V and unmodulated centre frequency fc≈455kHz recorded. Vv varied from -5.0V to +5.0V in 1.0V steps. At each step, steady-state frequency recorded, Δf = fout - fc computed and sensitivity Kf = Δf/Vi determined. Output frequency versus input voltage plotted to verify linearity, as in Table 304.1 and Graph 304.1.

DC source disconnected and audio function generator connected to FM2 input, configured for 1.0kHz sine with zero DC offset. DC offset checked with DMM to ensure 0.0V, as residual offset would shift fc and skew Δf calculations.

Oscilloscope CH1 connected to audio generator and CH2 to FM output. Trigger set to CH1 (audio). Triggering on FM output causes blurred display due to frequency jitter. Timebase adjusted to observe multiple audio cycles. Compression of RF cycles during positive audio peaks (higher frequency) and expansion during negative troughs (lower frequency) observed.

Audio amplitude varied from 0.5Vp-p to 6.0Vp-p in steps. For each level, fmax and fmin measured using counter, peak deviation Δf=(fmax-fmin)/2 calculated, modulation index β=Δf/fm and Carson bandwidth BW=2(Δf+fm) computed as in Table 304.2. At 6Vp-p, deviation 75.6kHz matching broadcast standard ±75kHz was obtained.
Carrier selector switched to Low (30kHz) and FM signal re-observed. Frequency variations became more visually pronounced, with cycle compression and expansion clearly distinguishable.
precautions: DC and peak AC voltages applied to FM inputs kept within ±6.0V to stay within linear tuning range. Exceeding this drives varactor diode into saturation or forward conduction causing non-linear distortion.
Audio generator DC offset set to 0.0V for dynamic AC test to avoid shifting resting carrier frequency from 455kHz and skewing Δf calculations.
Oscilloscope triggered on CH1 (audio modulating signal). Triggering on FM output causes display to blur into solid band due to continuous frequency jitter.
content.discussion:
Static VCO calibration (Table 304.1 and Graph 304.1) showed linear tuning across -5V to +5V. Measured sensitivity was about Kf=25.21kHz/V ±0.4%. Linearity is important because non-linearity in Kf would cause deviation to be non-linear with audio amplitude, producing harmonic distortion after discriminator detection. Beyond linear range (|Vi|>7V), varactor capacitance becomes non-linear (Cj ∝ (V0+VR)^-1/2) and slope flattens, as noted in manual.

Dynamic AC tests (Table 304.2) confirmed direct proportionality between modulating amplitude and frequency deviation. At Vin=6.0Vp-p (Vm=3.0V peak), measured deviation was Δf=75.60kHz, matching theoretical Δf=Kf*Vm=25.21*3.0=75.63kHz, error 0.04%. This matches standard ±75kHz deviation specified for commercial VHF FM broadcast by FCC and ITU, showing trainer mimics real broadcast specifications.

Comparison of FM and AM bandwidth illustrates fundamental trade-off: For AM with fm=1kHz, BW=2kHz. For FM with Δf=75.6kHz, Carson gives BW=2(75.6+1.0)=153.2kHz, about 76 times wider than AM. This extra bandwidth provides improved noise rejection because noise mainly affects amplitude and limiter removes it without affecting zero-crossing information. This is why FM is used for high-fidelity audio despite larger spectrum usage.

Time-domain observation showed dense RF cycles during positive audio peaks (higher instantaneous frequency) and sparse cycles during negative troughs (lower frequency). At high carrier 455kHz this is subtle, but at low carrier 30kHz it is visually obvious and helps understand instantaneous frequency concept.

Frequency counter readings fluctuated slightly (±0.2kHz) due to noise and supply ripple, so averaging was used. Proper triggering on audio input was essential for stable display; triggering on FM output initially gave blurred solid band until corrected.

The constant-envelope property was verified by observing that output amplitude remained constant while frequency varied, unlike AM where amplitude varies. This property allows efficient Class-C amplification.

Overall, VCO linearity, deviation proportionality to amplitude, independence from modulating frequency, and Carson bandwidth were verified experimentally.

content.conclusion:
VCO transfer characteristic confirmed linear conversion sensitivity Kf=25.21kHz/V across ±5V range. Dynamic tests showed frequency deviation Δf proportional to modulating amplitude Vm and independent of modulating frequency fm. Modulation index β=Δf/fm and Carson bandwidth BW=2(Δf+fm) were verified. At 6Vp-p input, broadcast-standard deviation of ±75.6kHz and bandwidth of 153.2kHz were obtained, about 76 times wider than AM for same audio, demonstrating trade-off between bandwidth and noise immunity that makes FM suitable for high-fidelity audio transmission. Proper triggering and DC offset control were found essential for accurate FM measurements.

questions.question: How does the VCO constant \(\mathit{K}_{f}\) vary with input voltage? Explain based on your calibration graph.
questions.answer: In ideal VCO, Kf=Δf/ΔVi is constant, so fout=fc+Kf Vi is linear. Experimental data in Table 304.1 and Graph 304.1 showed Kf between 25.00 and 25.30kHz/V across -5V to +5V, variation less than ±0.6%, essentially constant and linear. Beyond linear range (|Vi|>7V), varactor junction capacitance shows non-linear saturation, slope flattens and Kf decreases. Within ±5V used in lab, VCO operates in linear region suitable for low-distortion FM.

questions.question: What happens to the frequency deviation (\(\Delta f\) or \(\mathit{f}_{d}\)) when the input modulating amplitude increases? What happens when the modulating frequency increases?
questions.answer: When modulating amplitude Vm increases, Δf increases linearly as Δf=Kf Vm. Larger voltage swing drives varactor through wider capacitance range, giving larger frequency excursion. At 0.5Vp-p Δf=6.3kHz, at 6Vp-p Δf=75.6kHz, proportional. When modulating frequency fm increases, Δf remains unchanged because deviation depends only on amplitude, not rate of variation. However, β=Δf/fm decreases and Carson bandwidth BW=2Δf+2fm increases.

questions.question: Why does FM require substantially more transmission bandwidth than AM?
questions.answer: AM is linear multiplication: single audio fm with carrier fc produces only two sidebands fc-fm and fc+fm, bandwidth 2fm independent of modulation depth. FM is non-linear angle modulation: v(t)=Vc cos[ωc t+β sin(ωm t)] expands to Bessel series with infinite sideband pairs at ±fm, ±2fm, ±3fm, etc. To transmit without significant distortion, Carson's rule requires BW=2(Δf+fm)=2fm(β+1). For large β>>1, bandwidth dominated by 2Δf, requiring channels ten to eighty times wider than AM. Hence FM broadcast channels are 200kHz versus AM 10kHz.

questions.question: State four major engineering advantages of FM communication over AM in telecommunication systems.
questions.answer:
• Superior noise immunity: Atmospheric and industrial noise mainly affect amplitude. FM receiver limiter clips amplitude variations before discrimination.
• Constant power and high efficiency: FM envelope constant, so transmitter can use non-linear Class-C amplifiers with >80% efficiency versus AM requiring linear Class-A/AB with low efficiency.
• Capture effect: Co-channel interference results in receiver capturing stronger signal and suppressing weaker by up to 30dB, avoiding beat interference.
• Higher fidelity: FM supports wider audio bandwidth (50Hz-15kHz) and higher SNR (>70dB), suitable for high-fidelity stereo broadcast.

questions.question: Explain the "Bessel Null Technique" (Carrier Disappearance Method) used for ultra-precise laboratory calibration of frequency deviation meters.
questions.answer: In Bessel expansion, carrier amplitude at fc is Vc*J0(β) where J0 is zero-order Bessel function. J0(β) has zeros at β1=2.4048, β2=5.5201, β3=8.6537, β4=11.7915. In calibration, spectrum analyzer centred on fc, precise fm applied, modulating voltage Vm increased from zero while observing carrier spike. When carrier vanishes into noise floor, β is known precisely as 2.4048 for first null. Deviation is then Δf=β1*fm=2.4048*fm. Since calibration depends on mathematical constant rather than meter linearity, Bessel Null Technique is primary standard for deviation meter calibration.

learnings: Understanding of angle modulation where information is encoded in zero-crossing rate rather than amplitude, contrasting with AM.
Measurement of VCO transfer characteristic, determination of conversion gain Kf and assessment of linearity limits important for PLL and frequency synthesizer design.
Verification of Carson's bandwidth rule linking time-domain deviation to frequency-domain occupancy and trade-off between bandwidth and SNR.
Insight into wideband versus narrowband FM trade-offs and why FM is preferred for high-fidelity audio despite larger bandwidth requirement.
